transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
France's prime minister is asking local officials to impose limited curfews after unrest spread
across France.
Protests have been going on for weeks.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports French President Emmanuel Macron says delinquents should be
punished, not peaceful protesters.
Just remember, this started as a student protest over better conditioned and has widened to
include public sector workers against skyrocketing energy prices, high cost of living, inequality
in society.
But Macron didn't really give any concrete proposals.
He's leaving that to his prime minister, so he was immediately eviscerated by the left
and the right for not being tough enough and not offering solutions.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reporting.
Iran appointed a new defense minister yesterday.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shelchi reports Iranian officials say he will rebuild Iran's military after
U.S. and Israeli strikes.
Sixty-eight-year-old Mehdad Akhleri Khetabchi is a ballistic missile as an aerospace technology
expert with more than 42 years of military experience, according to Iranian officials.
He has strong ties to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and is sanctioned by the United
Nations and the U.S. for being an architect of Iran's missile industry.
He replaces Aziz Nasrzadeh, who was killed in U.S.-Israeli strikes on the first day of
the war, along with Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian
officials.
The Iranian defense ministry said that one of Khetabchi's priorities will be to replace
damaged weapons.
The U.S. has reportedly said that it has destroyed much of Iran's military capabilities.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
President Trump is continuing his campaign stops with Republican candidates this week
ahead of the midterm elections.
And Pierre Chandelis Duster has more.
President Trump is hitting the campaign trail again this week in hopes of giving Republican
candidates a boost ahead of the midterm elections.
Last month, he promised to visit 35 battleground districts to help Republican candidates.
And while he has said he would focus on swing districts, the majority of places where he
is campaigning are in Republican-heavy areas.
He is also visiting places where he made big wins during the 2024 presidential election.
One of his stops include North Carolina, where he will rally for Senate candidate Michael
Watley.
But Republicans have pulled back funding for ads for Watley across the state.
A sign of concern is Watley trails in the polls behind Democrat and former Governor
Roy Cooper.
Chandelis Duster, NPR News.
Police in Washington, D.C., say a National Guard member has been shot and wounded in
the leg.
The D.C. police chief says the Guard member was with several other troops when they were
trying to break up a fight amongst a group of people on a sidewalk.
The chief says a suspect shot and injured the Guard member, and other Guard members
opened fire, wounding the suspect.
No injury is life-threatening.
This is NPR.
NPR has lost one of its own.
From NPR News, it's all things considered.
I'm Noah Adams.
Noah Adams, a longtime host of All Things Considered, has died after a long illness.
He was 84 years old.
NPR's Scott Detrow has our remembrance.
Adams hosted the show for 18 years across two stints, helping listeners process 9/11
and the fall of the Berlin Wall, among other big stories.
But it was the quiet features where Adams left his mark.
Longtime All Things Considered host Melissa Block worked alongside him as a producer.
He was always observing, and he would have a little reporter's notebook, and he would
be taking notes in shorthand.
But somehow, when we came back, he would capture the character of a place or a person or a
town in the most vivid, rich, simple language.
Adams wrote books, too, including a memoir about learning to play piano in his 50s, and
he never stopped being a reporter.
His last piece for NPR aired just last month.
Scott Detrow, NPR News, Washington.
Canadian investigators are trying to find why a fire swept through a military base so
quickly on Saturday.
It was in the province of Alberta.
Four Canadian soldiers were killed, and 39 others were hurt.
Pope Leo gave his regular Sunday blessing yesterday in public at the Vatican.
It's been less than a week since he was hospitalized for cancer surgery and had part of a lung removed.
The pontiff was discharged Saturday.
Leo says he'll gradually resume his activities.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: France's prime minister asks local officials to impose limited curfews amid widening unrest
Macron says delinquents, not peaceful protesters, should be punished amid French protests
Iran appoints Mehdad Akhlaghi Khatibchi as defense minister to rebuild military after strikes
Trump resumes midterm campaign stops with Republican candidates, including Michael Whatley in North Carolina
Police say National Guard member shot in leg in Washington, D.C., suspect wounded
NPR remembers longtime All Things Considered host Noah Adams, who died at 84
Canadian investigators probe why fire swept through Alberta military base, killing four soldiers
Pope Leo gives Sunday blessing at Vatican less than a week after cancer surgery
